definition: An artificial brain (or artificial mind) is software and hardware with cognitive abilities similar to those of the animal or human brain.
details: Research investigating "artificial brains" and brain emulation plays three important roles in science: An ongoing attempt by neuroscientists to understand how the human brain works, known as cognitive neuroscience. A thought experiment in the philosophy of artificial intelligence, demonstrating that it is possible, at least in theory, to create a machine that has all the capabilities of a human being. A long-term project to create machines exhibiting behavior comparable to those of animals with complex central nervous system such as mammals and most particularly humans. The ultimate goal of creating a machine exhibiting human-like behavior or intelligence is sometimes called strong AI. An example of the first objective is the project reported by Aston University in Birmingham, England where researchers are using biological cells to create "neurospheres" (small clusters of neurons) in order to develop new treatments for diseases including Alzheimer's, motor neurone and Parkinson's disease. The second objective is a reply to arguments such as John Searle's Chinese room argument, Hubert Dreyfus's critique of AI or Roger Penrose's argument in The Emperor's New Mind. These critics argued that there are aspects of human consciousness or expertise that can not be simulated by machines. One reply to their arguments is that the biological processes inside the brain can be simulated to any degree of accuracy. This reply was made as early as 1950, by Alan Turing in his classic paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence". The third objective is generally called artificial general intelligence by researchers. However, Ray Kurzweil prefers the term "strong AI". In his book The Singularity is Near, he focuses on whole brain emulation using conventional computing machines as an approach to implementing artificial brains, and claims (on grounds of computer power continuing an exponential growth trend) that this could be done by 2025. Henry Markram, director of the Blue Brain project (which is attempting brain emulation), made a similar claim (2020) at the Oxford TED conference in 2009.

explainer.lead: An artificial brain is an attempt to give software and hardware cognitive abilities like those of an animal or human brain. The idea connects efforts to understand biological brains, test whether human capabilities could exist in a machine, and work toward human-like artificial intelligence.

tiers.eli5: Imagine building a machine that can think a bit like a person or an animal, rather than simply following instructions for one narrow job. Scientists could learn from real brains and try to reproduce their processes in software and hardware. This could also help us understand brains and explore diseases, but thinking like a human remains a long-term goal.
tiers.practitioner: Work on artificial brains centres on brain emulation and research systems rather than a standard, deployable engineering component. Approaches in the entry include simulating biological brain processes on conventional computers and growing small clusters of biological neurons called neurospheres for disease research. Do not treat forecasts about human-like machines as demonstrated capabilities.
tiers.paperLevel: Artificial brain = software + hardware with cognitive abilities similar to those of an animal or human brain; the ultimate goal of human-like behaviour or intelligence is sometimes called strong AI. Alan Turing's 1950 paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" gave an early reply to objections to machine intelligence by arguing that biological brain processes could, in principle, be simulated to any degree of accuracy. The concept remains tied to long-term brain-emulation research and to unresolved arguments about whether machines can reproduce human consciousness or expertise.

explainer.example: At Aston University in Birmingham, researchers use biological cells to create neurospheres, which are small clusters of neurons. Their work aims to develop new treatments for diseases including Alzheimer's, motor neurone and Parkinson's disease, illustrating the brain-understanding side of artificial-brain research.

explainer.intuition: Instead of designing intelligence only around a particular task, an artificial brain aims to reproduce enough of a biological brain's processes to obtain broader cognitive abilities. It can refer both to a research goal and to the software-and-hardware system that goal would produce.
howItWorks: Study the biological brain to understand the processes behind cognition.
Treat simulation of those processes as a possible route to machine capabilities.
Implement the emulation in software and hardware, including conventional computers.
Pursue increasingly complex animal-like and ultimately human-like behaviour.
Use related biological models such as neurospheres to investigate brain disease.
explainer.whyItMatters: Artificial brains link three major questions: how biological brains work, whether human capabilities can in principle exist in machines, and how machines might achieve general intelligence. They also connect philosophical arguments about consciousness with practical neuroscience and brain-emulation projects.
misconceptions: An artificial brain is not simply any AI program; the goal is cognition comparable to an animal or human brain.
Strong AI and artificial general intelligence describe the long-term goal, not an established result.
Kurzweil's 2025 and Markram's 2020 dates were predictions, not evidence that whole-brain emulation had been achieved.
Neurosphere disease research is an example of brain investigation, not a demonstration of a human-like artificial mind.
